fixes.explanation: Yes. The Teacher says "…the years approach of which you will say, 'I find no pleasure in them,'" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). That's what a person says about those years. It's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly: I think it's meant to make us listen.

That's the opposite of what the text says. The Teacher says "…the years approach of which you will say, 'I find no pleasure in them,'" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). Nobody in this verse is begging for those years to last. They are years the person says have no pleasure in them.

Not in this verse. The text says "…the years approach of which you will say, 'I find no pleasure in them,'" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The Teacher had already said that youth and vigor are fleeting (Ecclesiastes 11:10). These are different years.
False is right. The verse says, "…before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain…" The clouds come back. That's a gray picture, friend.
False, and you read that right. The verse says the keepers of the house tremble "…and the strong men stoop…" The strong men are bent over. Even the strong ones in this picture are bowing low, friend.

That's right. The verse says, "…when those grinding cease because they are few…" The work stops because those grinding are few. It's like a bakery shift where everybody went home and left me alone with the mixer. Wait, I'm alone with the mixer every day.
Yes, the bird. The verse says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" In the Teacher's picture, that's the sound a person rises at. Just a bird, friend, and up the person goes.
No bell in this verse. The text says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" A person rises at the sound of a bird, not a bell. Bells are lovely, but they aren't in this line.
Nice try, but no watchman is calling out here. The verse says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" Just a bird, friend. That's the sound named in this line.

False is right. The verse says, "…when men fear the heights and dangers of the road…" Nobody is bolder here, friend. They fear the heights and the dangers of the road. I think we all know a ladder that looks taller than it did last year.
That's it. The verse says "…for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets." The Teacher says it quietly and plainly. It's a heavy line, friend.
No Egypt here. The text says "…for then man goes to his eternal home…" Egypt isn't mentioned anywhere in this verse, friend. Mourners are walking the streets in it, so it's a serious one.
Right on. The silver cord is "snapped," the golden bowl is "crushed," the pitcher is "shattered" and the wheel is "broken" (Ecclesiastes 12:6). Four different things, and each one is broken.

Not every one. The cord is silver and the bowl is golden, but the verse doesn't say what the pitcher or the wheel are made of. What they all share is that each one is broken: snapped, crushed, shattered and broken (Ecclesiastes 12:6).

That's not what the verse says, friend. It says the silver cord is "snapped," the golden bowl is "crushed," the pitcher is "shattered" and the wheel is "broken" (Ecclesiastes 12:6). Being broken is what the four share. The verse says nothing about any of them being new.

True. The last line of the passage says, "'Futility of futilities,' says the Teacher. 'Everything is futile!'" It's a hard thing to end on, and it comes right after the Teacher's pictures of the dust and the spirit (Ecclesiastes 12:7). I think it's worth sitting with for a second.
